issues.legal_issue: A purchaser’s failure to meet expressly fixed payment dates may justify cancellation and defeat specific performance when the agreement makes payment time essential and the payment schedule was not varied.
material_facts: The agreement required payment of the balance price in specified instalments and expressly made payment on the due dates essential, with cancellation available for default.
The purchaser missed part of the second instalment and the entire final instalment.
The courts found that the parties had not agreed to postpone the instalments until the sellers produced original title documents.
The agreement made the timing of the sale deed depend on the purchaser’s convenience but did not make the payment schedule depend on further title review.
issues.conclusion: The sellers were justified in cancelling the agreement, and the purchaser was not entitled to specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 55 of the Contract Act, 1872 governs failure to perform at a fixed time when time is essential. For sales of immovable property, time is generally presumed not to be essential, but that presumption may be displaced by the contract’s express terms and circumstances. Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani, relying on Gomathinayagam Pillai v. Pallaniswami Nadar and Govind Prasad Chaturvedi v. Hari Dutt Shastri, states that fixing a performance period alone is insufficient, but unequivocal terms may make time essential. K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan supports giving significance to stipulated periods, applying greater scrutiny to readiness and willingness, and not treating the limitation period as permission to delay. The Court noted that rising property values and prolonged litigation make mechanical reliance on the general presumption inappropriate, while leaving a general reconsideration of the rule for another case. N. Srinivasa v. Kuttukaran Machine Tools Ltd. was distinguished as a conclusion based on that contract’s terms, not a categorical rule that time can never be essential.

rule.if: specific_performance_case and payment_dates_fixed and payment_time_made_essential and purchaser_missed_due_payments and no_agreed_payment_variation

predicates.specific_performance_case: The proceeding sought specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.payment_dates_fixed: The agreement set dates for payment of the balance price.
predicates.payment_time_made_essential: The agreement stated that payment on the specified dates was essential and provided for cancellation on default.
predicates.purchaser_missed_due_payments: The purchaser failed to pay some or all instalments when due.
predicates.no_agreed_payment_variation: The parties did not agree to change the payment schedule.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance proceeding concerns an agreement with fixed, essential payment dates, and the purchaser misses payments without an agreed change to the schedule, the rule treats cancellation as valid and specific performance as unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser cannot postpone an unconditional payment obligation until the seller produces title documents when the agreement does not make payment conditional on title satisfaction or fix that order of performance.
material_facts: The agreement separately required payment of the balance price by specified dates and provided that execution of the sale deed would depend on the purchaser’s satisfaction regarding title and encumbrances.
The agreement did not state that payment depended on title satisfaction or that the sellers had to produce original title documents before payment.
The sellers were to use the sale proceeds to discharge loans and obtain the original documents.
The agreement provided for repayment of advances if the purchaser notified the sellers of dissatisfaction with title and the sellers failed to satisfy her.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser had to pay the balance price as agreed and could not withhold it pending production of the original title documents.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 51 to 54 of the Contract Act, 1872 govern reciprocal promises. Under section 52, the order of performance is determined by an order expressly fixed in the contract or, if none is fixed, by the nature of the transaction; the order in which clauses appear in a written agreement does not itself fix that order. Section 54 prevents a party from claiming a reciprocal promise when that party has failed to perform the promise that must come first. Sections 51 and 53 address simultaneous performance and prevention of performance. The Court held that the payment obligation here was unconditional and preceded the sellers’ obligation to obtain and produce the original title deeds.

predicates.sale_contract_dispute: The proceeding concerns the parties’ respective obligations under an agreement to sell property.
predicates.payment_obligation_unconditional: The agreement requires the purchaser to pay on specified terms without making payment conditional on another act by the seller.
predicates.title_satisfaction_conditions_only_sale_: The agreement makes title satisfaction a condition for completing the sale deed, rather than for paying the balance price.
predicates.agreement_does_not_fix_title_documents_b: The agreement does not expressly require the seller to produce title documents before the purchaser pays.

issues.definition: Where an agreement to sell makes payment unconditional, makes title satisfaction relevant only to the sale deed, and does not require title documents before payment, the purchaser must pay as agreed before demanding those documents.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser is not entitled to an extension of the payment period on a fraud theory when suppression of encumbrances was neither pleaded nor proved and the purchaser knew of the encumbrances.
material_facts: The purchaser alleged that the sellers had concealed mortgages and that this prevented timely payment.
The plaint did not specifically plead fraud, and the evidence did not establish deliberate concealment.
The purchaser and her representatives had examined copies of title documents before contracting and knew of the encumbrances.
The unpaid instalments could have enabled the sellers to discharge the relevant debts and obtain the original documents.
issues.conclusion: The alleged suppression did not establish fraud or entitle the purchaser to an extension of time, and the sellers’ cancellation was justified.
issues.legal_principle: Section 55(1) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, requires a seller to disclose a material defect in the property or title that the seller knows and the buyer does not know and could not discover with ordinary care, and to produce title documents in the seller’s possession or power on request. Section 34 of that Act allows further time where fraud by a person benefited by non-fulfilment prevents performance within the specified time. Fraud must be specifically pleaded and proved. The Court found neither the necessary pleading and proof nor concealment of an unknown encumbrance on these facts.

rule.if: sale_contract_dispute and fraud_relied_on_to_extend_payment_time and fraud_not_pleaded_or_proved and purchaser_knew_of_encumbrances

predicates.sale_contract_dispute: The proceeding concerns performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.fraud_relied_on_to_extend_payment_time: The purchaser relies on alleged fraud by the seller as a reason to extend the time for payment.
predicates.fraud_not_pleaded_or_proved: The purchaser did not specifically plead fraud or establish it with evidence.
predicates.purchaser_knew_of_encumbrances: The purchaser or the purchaser’s representatives knew of the relevant encumbrances before contracting.

issues.definition: When a purchaser seeks more time to pay based on alleged seller fraud but does not plead or prove fraud and knew of the encumbrances, the rule denies an extension on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A court should not draw an adverse inference from a party’s failure to testify when a representative with complete knowledge of the transaction gives evidence on that party’s behalf.
material_facts: The three owners did not testify personally.
The transaction had been conducted on their behalf by a family member who had complete knowledge of it.
That representative testified about the transaction, while the owners lacked full or complete knowledge of its details.
issues.conclusion: No adverse inference was warranted from the owners’ failure to testify.
issues.legal_principle: Man Kaur v. Hartar Singh Sangha explains that where an agent or representative handled the entire transaction, that person may give evidence about it, particularly when the principal had no personal knowledge. The Court distinguished the reliance placed on Vidhyadhar v. Mankikrao and Balasaheb Dayandeo Naik v. Appasaheb Dattatraya Pawar because a knowledgeable representative had testified.

rule.if: civil_case and party_did_not_testify and knowledgeable_transaction_representative_testified and party_lacked_full_personal_knowledge

predicates.civil_case: The proceeding is a civil case involving disputed facts about a transaction.
predicates.party_did_not_testify: A party to the proceeding did not personally give evidence.
predicates.knowledgeable_transaction_representative: A representative who handled or knew the transaction gave evidence about it.
predicates.party_lacked_full_personal_knowledge: The absent party did not have full personal knowledge of the transaction.

issues.definition: If a party in a civil case does not testify but a knowledgeable representative gives evidence about the transaction and the party lacks full personal knowledge, the rule does not permit an adverse inference merely from the party’s absence.

issues.legal_issue: A caretaker who was never given possession under an agreement to sell cannot obtain a permanent injunction to protect possession after the agreement is cancelled.
material_facts: The agreement entrusted the property to the purchaser only as caretaker until the full price was paid and possession was delivered.
The purchaser did not pay the full price, and the sellers did not deliver possession in part performance.
The agreement was validly cancelled.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was not entitled to a permanent injunction, and dismissal of the injunction suit was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished possession delivered in part performance from custody as a caretaker under the agreement. Because the purchaser never had possession, there was no possession for a permanent injunction to protect; cancellation also ended the caretaker arrangement.

rule.if: permanent_injunction_case and claimant_received_property_only_as_caretaker and possession_never_delivered_to_claimant and agreement_cancelled

predicates.permanent_injunction_case: The proceeding seeks a permanent injunction protecting the claimant’s asserted possession of property.
predicates.claimant_received_property_only_as_caret: The claimant was entrusted with the property only to care for it for the owner.
predicates.possession_never_delivered_to_claimant: The owner did not deliver possession to the claimant, including in part performance of the sale agreement.
predicates.agreement_cancelled: The agreement under which the caretaker held the property was cancelled.

issues.definition: If a claimant in a permanent-injunction case held property only as caretaker, never received possession, and the agreement was cancelled, the rule denies an injunction to protect possession.

issues.legal_issue: Amounts paid under a sale transaction must be repaid with interest from cancellation when the agreement provides no forfeiture and the sellers have undertaken to refund the amounts.
material_facts: The purchaser paid advances to the sellers and a further sum to another recipient, which the courts found was consideration for movables.
The agreement contained no provision allowing forfeiture of the advances and provided for repayment in a specified title-related circumstance.
The sellers offered to refund the amounts in their written statement, subject to conditions.
The Court found that the purchaser had not brought false, frivolous, or mischievous suits, so the refund condition relied on by the sellers did not bar repayment.
The sellers’ repayment obligation was independent of the purchaser’s caretaker role.
issues.conclusion: The repayment decree was upheld, with interest running from cancellation rather than only for the period when the purchaser was not acting as caretaker, and at the increased rate ordered by the Court.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the agreement’s lack of a forfeiture provision, its repayment term, and the sellers’ written offer to refund. It held that the condition attached to the offer did not defeat repayment because the purchaser had not filed false, frivolous, or mischievous suits. The refund obligation was not linked to the caretaker arrangement, so interest ran from cancellation. The Court adjusted the rate of interest in light of the facts and circumstances.

rule.if: refund_dispute_after_sale_agreement_cancellation and purchaser_paid_transaction_amounts and agreement_has_no_forfeiture_term and seller_offered_refund and refund_offer_condition_not_triggered

predicates.refund_dispute_after_sale_agreement_canc: The proceeding concerns repayment after an agreement to sell was cancelled.
predicates.purchaser_paid_transaction_amounts: The purchaser paid amounts to the sellers or another recipient in connection with the transaction.
predicates.agreement_has_no_forfeiture_term: The agreement does not provide that the amounts paid may be forfeited.
predicates.seller_offered_refund: The seller undertook in the proceeding to repay the amounts received.
predicates.refund_offer_condition_not_triggered: The facts required to defeat the seller’s refund undertaking did not occur.

issues.definition: When a purchaser paid transaction amounts, the agreement has no forfeiture term, and a seller’s refund undertaking is not defeated by its condition, the rule requires repayment with interest from cancellation.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser cannot recover a sum as commission from its recipient when the courts find that it was paid as consideration for movables and the purchaser did not pursue that claim on appeal.
material_facts: The purchaser sued the recipient of the sum, claiming it had been paid as commission and seeking its return.
The trial court found that the sum was consideration for movables, not commission.
On appeal, the purchaser’s counsel stated that the claim against the recipient was not being pressed in light of that finding.
issues.conclusion: The dismissal of the purchaser’s recovery claim against the recipient was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The Court upheld the factual finding about the purpose of the payment and relied on the purchaser’s statement that the claim against the recipient was not being pressed. It identified no separate statutory rule governing this disposition.

predicates.recovery_claim_against_payment_recipient: The proceeding seeks repayment of a sum from the person who received it.
predicates.payment_found_to_be_consideration_for_go: The court finds that the payment was consideration for goods or movables rather than the claimed commission.
predicates.claimant_did_not_press_claim_on_appeal: The claimant’s counsel states on appeal that the claim against the recipient is not being pursued.

issues.definition: When a repayment claim against a payment recipient concerns a sum found to be consideration for movables and the claimant does not pursue the claim on appeal, the rule upholds dismissal of that claim.

issues.legal_issue: A memorandum of understanding to enter a future sale agreement after litigation is resolved, and advances paid under it, do not by themselves create an encumbrance in breach of an order prohibiting encumbrances.
material_facts: An interim order prohibited the owners from encumbering the property.
The owners were alleged to have executed memoranda of understanding agreeing to enter into sale agreements later, after pending litigation was resolved.
The memoranda did not themselves constitute agreements of sale, and advances were allegedly paid under them.
The contempt applicants alleged that the memoranda were backdated, but produced no material establishing that allegation.
issues.conclusion: The memoranda and alleged advances did not amount to encumbering the property or violating the interim order, and the contempt petitions were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: An encumbrance is a charge or burden created by transferring an interest in property and is a liability attached to the property that runs with the land. National Textile Corporation v. State of Maharashtra and State of H.P. v. Tarsem Singh were relied on for that understanding. A memorandum merely agreeing to enter a future sale agreement after litigation is resolved, and receipt of advances under it, do not themselves transfer an interest or create an encumbrance.

predicates.contempt_proceeding_for_breach_of_no_enc: The proceeding alleges contempt of an order prohibiting a party from encumbering property.
predicates.document_only_promises_future_sale_agree: The document only records an intention to enter a sale agreement after pending litigation is resolved.
predicates.no_interest_in_property_transferred: The document and related payments do not transfer an interest in the property.

issues.definition: When contempt is alleged for breach of a no-encumbrance order but the document only promises a future sale agreement after litigation and transfers no property interest, the rule finds no encumbrance breach and dismisses contempt.
